analysis.investment_thesis: CESC is a regulated electricity utility with stable but deeply unexciting economics: nine-year net profit CAGR of 7.8%, ROE of 11.3%, and borrowings that have surged from INR 14,544 Cr to INR 18,811 Cr in a single year to fund renewable capex — this is precisely the kind of capital-heavy, low-return, high-debt business I avoid. The valuation at 15.4x P/E is not compelling enough to offset the structural negatives.
key_strengths: Regulated monopoly in the Kolkata distribution area provides absolute revenue floor — electricity demand is non-discretionary and predictable
OCF positive all five years (INR 1,978–3,408 Cr range) demonstrating real cash generation at the operating level
Net profit has compounded steadily if slowly (INR 729 Cr to INR 1,428 Cr over nine years) — no year of loss, which speaks to the regulated-return model
key_risks: D/E of 1.41 is far beyond my maximum; borrowings jumped from INR 14,544 Cr to INR 18,811 Cr in FY25, driven by a capex surge to INR 1,863 Cr — almost 2.5x the prior year's level
Revenue CAGR of 3.8% over nine years and operating income declining at -1.6% CAGR signals a business being left behind by inflation — in real terms, it is shrinking
FCF has collapsed from INR 2,495 Cr (FY20) to INR 729 Cr (FY25) as capex ramps up; free cash yield is deteriorating rapidly
red_flags: Other income has grown at 34% CAGR and now INR 1,618 Cr in FY25 — nearly as large as reported operating income of INR 2,849 Cr; the quality of core earnings is questionable when one-time or non-operating gains prop up the P&L
Borrowings surging in a single year by INR 4,267 Cr to fund renewable projects is aggressive expansion funded by debt — a direct violation of my investing principles
Promoter at 52.11% — barely above majority, leaving little buffer and limited skin-in-the-game conviction
analysis.detailed_analysis: CESC's regulated electricity franchise in Kolkata is a genuine asset, but the current strategy of aggressively bidding renewable projects (300 MW solar, 450 MW hybrid in Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh) funded by substantial new debt transforms a predictable utility into a leveraged growth bet. That is not a combination I find appealing. The operating income is declining in absolute terms even as revenue rises — regulatory tariff squeezes are eating the returns.
